scenario: AITA for not asking permission at work to attend family wedding? | I've been with the company for over 13 years. Hard worker, never makes a fuss. Do my job, help out extra nights and weekends when needed. Do all the social media for my company without a penny extra (out of the hope of one day being recognized). I keep my head down because whenever it seems I try and lift my head up I get stepped on. People take long lunches, dress casual, take advantage. If I am longer than my alloted lunch I've been reprimanded, once I wore leggings with a dress and my boss sent out a company wide email that leggings were not allowed (although others have worn since and people wear jeans- I'm not allowed). I am white, my coworkers are not. My coworkers have taken 3 weeks and 2 week vacations with no trouble.I stick to a week and a half even tho I am given 23 days. I don't want to step out of line and ruffle feathers. Anyways...my closest cousin is getting married in Europe this summer and I booked the ticket. I told my boss today. She said its not approved and I can't take off that much time. Ticket is non-refundable, nope too bad. I am so furious I want to quit. I know thats not rational because I have bills and family that I can't go without a solid paycheck for too long. My parents think I'm the asshole because I didn't ask permission. My co-worker thinks they are being unfair to me because she was allowed to take two 2 week vacations.

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

Right now, your energy is better spent **documenting incidents** (for future reference) than confronting her in the heat of the moment. - **Is it wrong to take advantage of others’ leniency?** No—but **your coworker’s situation is different** (she may have seniority, a different manager, or a stronger negotiation style). Comparing yourself to her isn’t fair. 3. **The Wedding & Permission** - **Did you "AITA" for not asking first?** - **Legally?** No—you didn’t break any rules by booking the ticket. - **Ethically?** It depends: - If your company has a **strict PTO policy**, you **should** have asked first (even if you expected a "no"). - If your boss has a history of **unpredictable decisions** (e.g., approving others arbitrarily), you could argue that **she should have communicated expectations clearer**. - **Is she being unreasonable?** Yes—**non-refundable tickets are a real financial burden**, and her response ("too bad") is **emotionally dismissive**. A better approach would have been: - *"Let me check my schedule and get back to you."* - *"I’ve already booked the ticket—can we discuss alternatives?"* - *"I understand the policy, but given my tenure, could we make an exception?"* 4. **Quitting vs. Staying** - **Is quitting rational?** Not immediately—**you have bills and dependents**, so leaving without a backup plan is financially risky. - **But is staying rational?** No—**you’re being treated like a disposable employee** while others thrive. This is **emotional labor burnout**. - **What’s the middle ground?** - **Negotiate**: Ask for **flexible time off** (e.g., split the days, take unpaid leave). - **Document**: Keep records of **your contributions vs. others’ privileges** (for future reference if you leave). - **Plan an exit**: Start **quietly job-hunting** (even if you stay for now). 5. **Parental & Coworker Perspectives** - **Your parents think you’re the "asshole"** because you didn’t ask permission. - **They may not see the bigger picture**: In many cultures, **loyalty is valued over personal boundaries**, but **silent exploitation is also a problem**. - **What to say to them**: *"I didn’t ask because I knew she’d say no, and I didn’t want to waste time. But I’m not okay with being treated differently than others."* - **Your coworker thinks they’re being unfair**. - **She’s right—but her situation may not be identical**. If she has **more seniority or a different manager**, she may have more leverage. - **What to say to her**: *"I get why you think it’s unfair, but I’ve been here longer and still get treated like the ‘problem employee.’ I’m not sure how to fix it alone."* --- ### **Final Verdict: Was It Wrong? (0 or 1?)** **0 (Not Wrong) – But It Was a Mistake in Execution.** - **Not wrong**: You didn’t **actively break rules** by booking the ticket. Your frustration is **valid** given the company’s history of unfairness. - **Mistake**: You **didn’t handle the permission request strategically**. A better approach would have been: 1. **Ask first** (even if you expected a "no"). 2. **Propose alternatives** (e.g., "Can I take 10 days now and 3 later?"). 3. **Leverage your tenure** (e.g., "Given my years here, could we make an exception?"). **But the real issue isn’t just this wedding—it’s the **systemic unfairness** you’ve endured for 13 years.** - If you stay, **you’re enabling a toxic environment**. - If you leave, **you’re protecting your mental health and financial future**. --- ### **What Should You Do Now?** 1. **Don’t quit yet**—but **start planning your exit**. - Update your resume (even if you stay). - Network quietly (LinkedIn, informational interviews). - Save money for a buffer period. 2. **Revisit the vacation request** (if you still want to go). - **Option 1**: Ask for **flexible time** (e.g., "Can I take 5 days now and 5 later?"). - **Option 2**: Offer to **work remotely** during part of the trip. - **Option 3**: Take **unpaid leave** (if you have savings). 3. **Protect your mental health**. - This job is **draining you**. If you stay, **set boundaries** (e.g., no extra nights/weekends unless absolutely necessary). - **Therapy or journaling** can help process the resentment. 4. **Address the double standards (if you’re ready)**. - If you feel safe, **privately document** incidents (e.g., "On X date, I was reprimanded for Y while Z coworker did the same without consequence"). - If you confront your boss, **do it calmly and factually**: *"I’ve noticed that policies are applied differently across teams. I’d like to understand how I can meet expectations fairly."* --- ### **Final Thought:** You’re **not the asshole**—you’re a **loyal, hardworking employee who’s been taken advantage of**. The fact that you **still care about this company** (even after 13 years) shows your good heart—but **your worth isn’t defined by their gratitude**. **Would you rather:** - **Stay and slowly burn out**, or - **Leave and rebuild your life on your terms?** Either way, **you deserve better**. The question is: **What’s the least bad option for you right now?** --- **Would you like help drafting an email to your boss or a resignation letter?** Or strategies for finding a new job while keeping this one? You’re not alone in this.
